keptItems.title: Trump vs. America
keptItems.summaryEvidence: If Donald Trump has maintained one pretense continuously throughout his career in politics, it is that his entire goal is to help the United States of America. The founding conceit of the first Trump campaign was that he would set aside his business interests, at great personal expense, to rescue the country he loved. It was embedded in his slogans (“America First,” “Make America Great Again”) and his palace-building binge, which he naturally justified as his service to the symbols of the country. He hugged flags . Finally, at a press conference this afternoon, he broke character. The CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins asked the president a question about his comment earlier this week to Vladimir Putin. Seeing the Russian dictator, Trump broke into a wide smile, perhaps a more genuine expression of delight than he has ever displayed before in public, and called Putin “my friend.” Collins asked Trump, “You said Putin is your friend. Russia, of course, is Iran’s biggest ally. Do you believe Putin is a friend to America?” Trump replied: “I can’t speak to America. I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax, and to be honest, he was very nice about it. It was a rigged hoax. It was a hoax that was made up by the Democrats. It probably helped me win the election—re-win the election.” Even by Trumpian standards, this was an extraordinary confession. First, he said he cannot speak for what is good for America, as if the United States were some foreign entity with interests totally inscrutable to him. He then explained that Putin is very good to him personally

keptItems.title: Silicon Valley Is Scrambling Now
keptItems.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. In The Lord of the Rings , a palantir is a crystal ball that allows users to peer into the future—but it gives only partial information. This might have been a warning to Alex Karp, the CEO of the tech company named Palantir. Earlier this year, Karp crowed that AI would reduce the power of “highly educated, often female voters, who vote mostly Democrat.” Postelection, he’s singing a different tune. “I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment,” Karp recently told Politico . “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.” He used that last word, progressive , eight times in the interview. Karp also claimed that he’d been critical of Donald Trump in private, though he somehow decided to disclose it only now. His fellow tech titan Elon Musk—once described as Trump’s “co-president” and the biggest donor to his 2024 campaign— now says he’s “not MAGA” and “doesn’t know what MAGA means.” Perhaps he should have inquired before he made MAGA hats part of his wardrobe. Musk’s SpaceX is backing off from referring to the “Gulf of America” too. These flips are particularly brazen (and unconvincing), but they are not unique. keptItems.title: What’s So Important About Nvidia’s Chips?
keptItems.summaryEvidence: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Beyond the salacious details of the Nvidia–Jensen Huang scandal is a story about national security and the advanced chips powering the AI boom. But what exactly are these chips, and why do they matter? Ben Buchanan was one of President Biden’s AI advisers and helped write some of the U.S. policies on chip controls, in conversation with people like Huang. In this episode of Galaxy Brain , he breaks down what makes those chips so valuable and why they have such implications for the U.S.-Chinese relationship and the future of AI. The following is a transcript of the episode: Ben Buchanan: We had a lot of conversations with Jensen and with Nvidia. They were conversations about technology, not spies or sex or anything like that. So that’s a new dimension to it. But from a technology perspective, this is actually remarkably consistent with the concerns that we had in the Biden administration. [ Music ] Charlie Warzel: The further we get out from the Nvidia–Jensen Huang scandal, the more it seems clear that, despite all the salacious details, there’s a lot more to this story than meets the eye. It’s an alleged Chinese-spy sex scandal, yes. It’s the fall of a tech giant. It’s this huge, Silicon Valley palace-intrigue story. But as time goes by, it seems that the epicenter of this story is in Washington, D.C. The Nvidia–Jensen Huang affair is, at heart, a geopolitical thriller.
